paragraphs.text: The London Bus Museum is popular with tourists and transport enthusiasts alike - but its history has not been straightforward. The origins of London bus preservation and collection go back to 1929 when the London General Omnibus Company assembled a few of its early buses as part of a celebration to mark a century of London bus operation. Following the success of this, those early buses were kept to one side for similar future use. After the formation of London Transport (LT) in 1933, further examples were added to this ‘commemorative fleet’.

The first known attempt at private preservation of a London bus was in the late 1940s when The Omnibus Society considered the purchase from LT of a G-wheeler double-decker bus, but negotiations broke down. A further go at private preservation was made in 1952 by one Prince Marshall, then aged 15, who tried to purchase a single-decker from LT but could not afford the £250 asking price. Despite this setback, he later joined with six other people to try again. Their group raised only £93 of the £100 required, so this attempt also failed. In 1956, progress was finally made, with the ecquisition from LT by a group of individuals, including some from the previous consortium, of a 1929 single-decker from London Transport. This was the moment when private preservation of buses in the UK began.By 1970, there were over 50 London buses in preservation in the UK, and today there are estimated to be over 5,000, both privately owned and in a large number of museums throughout the country.

By the mid-1960s, there was a handful of London buses in private preservation and a number of their owners came together in 1966 to form the London Bus Preservation Group. The objectives of the group were to co-ordinate efforts and knowledge, and to accumulate spare parts. The biggest problem private bus-owners faced at that time was locating secure, covered accommodation for buses. Many early preserved buses were kept in fields where their already poor condition deteriorated. A solution to this issue was found by the group in 1972, with the acquisition of what had been an aircraft factory at Cobham, roughly 50km outside London. Over the next few years, the group worked hard to turn the near-derelict building into a storage facility and workshop for some 35 buses. In 1974, the venue, by then called Cobham Bus Museum, held its first open day, an event which has been held annually ever since. Over the years that followed, the museum acquired several important historic London buses and restored a number of them to a high standard. Also started was the process of evolution from a bus preservation society toa proper museum, with a subsequent increase in membership. However, further progress was hampered by the deteriorating state of the building.

By the early 2000s, it became clear that radical action would have to be taken if the museum were to survive; the roof was leaking and the subsequent dampness levels were threatening the well-being of the buses. There was no prospect of obtaining planning permission to operate a museum open to the general public from the Cobham site, nor of finding the money to rebuild. This combination of problems threatened the group's status as a registered museum and charity, without which its financial future was very uncertain.

The group concluded that the only financial solution was to realise the value of the site, and to use the proceeds to acquire another site where a public museum could be operated. Luckily, the nearby Brooklands Museum proved willing to make available a large plot of vacant land where the group could erect a new museum building. A deal was concluded whereby the land would be acquired on a 125-year lease, and the visitor entrance and admission revenue would be shared between the two museums.

Site clearance for the new building began towards the end of 2010, with construction starting in January 2011. In May that year, the museum took possession of its gleaming new premises and, after a period of fitting out, the newly-named London Bus Museum opened its doors to the public on 1st August 2011. Finally, after many years of frustrations and uncertainty, the Museum had a secure, long-term future. It could now fulfil its destiny as the custodian of London's bus heritage with the ability to present this to the public, and to continue its restoration and conservation work in a proper, well-equipped environment. Today's magnificent London Bus Museum stands as a tribute to the foresight and efforts of the early pioneers such as Prince Marshall, without which none of this could have happened.
